title: Lamrim: all were our mothers
hookLine: seeing every being as having been one's mother in some life, and repaying their kindness

lines: A LONG LINE, COINS COUNTED SLOWLY.
SHE MAY HAVE BEEN YOUR MOTHER.
TRY IT ON AS A WORKING ASSUMPTION.
cards: The checkout line is long, and the woman ahead of you is counting coins out of a little purse, slowly, one at a time. Behind you somebody sighs loudly. You might be about to sigh too.

Here's a strange teaching from the Tibetan stages of the path. It says that woman, and the sigher behind you, and the pigeon outside the door, have each, at some time in the long round of lives, been your mother. Fed you.
Carried you. Stayed up with you. Not as a poem, but as a working assumption, to be tried on and lived with.

teach.b: First, the reasoning. Two days ago the lamrim looked at samsara, a round of lives with no beginning anyone can find.
If it has gone on that long, the teaching says, every being has at some point been close to you, and at some point been your mother.
The idea isn't only Tibetan: a discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya says it's not easy to find a being who has not, at some time in this long wandering, been one's mother.
Second, remembering kindness. The lamrim asks the student to recall a mother's care in detail: carried before birth, fed, cleaned, watched over, taught to speak and walk.

Some teachers know a listener's own mother may have been hard, absent or unkind, and suggest starting with whoever did care for you, a grandmother, a neighbor, a nurse. The kindness is the point, not the title.

teach.h: WANT TO REPAY: LOVE, COMPASSION, RESOLVE.
teach.b: Remembering a kindness that large, the student wants to give something back, and that wish opens into a run of steps: love, wishing beings happiness; compassion, wishing them free of suffering; and finally the resolve to awaken for their sake.
Tibetan teachers trace this sequence back to Atisha. Fourth, what it does on a Tuesday. Nobody can check a stranger's past lives; that's not the exercise.
The exercise is to treat the woman with the coins the way you'd treat someone who once rocked you to sleep.
Patience may come a little easier. The sigh behind you may sound different. For a minute, the checkout line holds a family nobody announced.

how: In Tibetan lamrim practice, students meditate step by step on all beings as having been their mothers, on their kindness and on the wish to repay it, as the ground for love, compassion and the resolve to awaken for others.

o: the next stair: honoring your own mother above all
the next stair: a belief that mothers are reborn as kin
the next stair: seeing every being as once your mother

games.q: the woman ahead of you in line is counting coins slowly, and you're in a hurry. the lamrim has a suggestion. which one?
o: treat her as someone who once cared for you.
switch lines and forget about her.
games.why: the teaching asks you to see her as having been your mother, and to repay that kindness, starting with patience.

practice: Bring to mind someone who cared for you when you were small, and let one specific kindness come back: a meal, a hand on your forehead, a ride home.
Then bring to mind a stranger you saw recently and try on the thought that this person once did that for you. You don't have to believe it; just see what changes in how you look at them.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim. The stages of the path. Today's stage: seeing all beings as having been our mothers, and wanting to repay their kindness. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan ma, mother. The lamrim speaks of all beings as 'mother sentient beings.'

carryVoice: Your line: all were our mothers. A stranger may be family nobody announced. See you tomorrow.
